sql_problem.title: The optimal polynomial lower bound on the edge-isoperimetric number of the graph square
sql_problem.difficulty_reason: Counted unit: original Theorem 3.7 of the article (source label theorem:lowerboundi(G^2)closed, source0.tex lines 357--367), the optimal closed-form lower bound on the edge-isoperimetric number $i(G^2)$ of the square of a non-complete regular connected graph, with its three cases for the optimal polynomial $p$ distinguished by the spectral quantities $\Lambda$, $M$, $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$ and $\lambda_n$. It is delivered with the authors' own complete 59-line proof at source0.tex lines 370--428. H2: the proof is a genuine optimisation of a spectral bound rather than a qualifying examination exercise. The solver must take the general polynomial $p=ax^2+bx+c$, translate the isoperimetric inequality of the general theorem into the three candidate regimes for the coefficients through the interlacing eigenvalues of $G^2$, compare the resulting rational expressions one by one, and identify in each case the polynomial that makes the bound sharp, obtaining the three displayed inequalities. Reproducing that case analysis of spectral bounds for the graph square is well beyond ordinary PhD qualifying level.

sql_problem.title: An exponential upper bound on the number of large sets with a small edge boundary in a product graph
sql_problem.difficulty_reason: The counted statement is the counting lemma for large sets with a small edge boundary (author lemma at source lines 714-716, label lem:small-boundary-sets): for a in the stated range, at most exp(2a/log d) sets of size a have an edge boundary below a log^2 d. The proof (source lines 718-743) has genuine content: it restricts to a sub-product on a set I of m = log_2(log^5 d) coordinates, applies the author's isoperimetric inequality on that sub-product to force any set with a small boundary to interact non-trivially with few of the fibres, converts that into a binomial-product bound on the number of admissible sets, and then optimises over m and over the choice of I to reach the exponential bound (proof lines 719-742). The lemma is one of the two counting inputs to the size bound on obstructions. H2.
